title: 2027 Audi SQ7: Prices, Reviews & Pictures - CarGurus.com
summary: Explore the 2027 Audi SQ7 with CarGurus reviews, pricing insights, comparisons, news and expert analysis.
body_markdown:
## Look & feel


8/10


Like the previous generation, the 2027 Audi SQ7 retains most of the styling of the Q7 midsize three-row SUV it’s based on, with detail changes that convey its sporty character.


With this third generation, the Q7 has morphed into an imposing but somewhat generic-looking SUV. There’s nothing car-like about its boxy profile, large size, and massive grille, and these are all things that convey that this is a luxury SUV. But there isn’t much that marks it as an Audi besides illuminated four-ring badges and clever headlights that finally incorporate the matrix technology Audi launched in Europe well over a decade ago.


Matrix lights aim individual elements away from oncoming cars and other road users rather than switching the high beams on and off. They’re paired with LED daytime running lights that can be programmed with different designs, and OLED taillights that can show warning triangles when the hazards are on (very tiny ones, though), and pulse to full brightness when someone approaches from behind too quickly. When equipped with the Luxury Package, the turn signals can also project arrows onto the road surface—even at highway speeds.


The SQ7 adds model-specific front and rear bumpers, a unique grille with what Audi calls a honeycomb pattern (it looks more like roof shingles to us), aluminum-look trim (black is also available, and standard 22-inch wheels (23s are also available). That doesn’t add up to much visual difference from the Q7, and the latter gets an S Line exterior trim package and Launch Edition trim that mimic some of the SQ7’s styling features. But that just makes this a SUV a true sleeper.


SQ7-specific interior features are mostly limited to color and material options. Like the base Q7, the interior feels appreciably more upscale thanks to good materials choices and a more cohesive design than other recent Audi models. The SQ7 is also equipped very similar to a fully-loaded Q7, with standard features like Nappa leather upholstery, power rear-window sunshades, and a panoramic glass sunroof with dimmable panels. None of these features are necessary in a performance vehicle, but they do make the SQ7 feel less bare-bones than a similarly-priced Porsche Cayenne.


## Performance


9/10


The SQ7 thoroughly distinguishes itself under the hood with an exclusive twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 connected to an eight-speed automatic transmission and performance-tuned all-wheel drive (AWD) system. All of that is the same as before, but the engine now produces 591 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque—91 hp and 22 lb-ft more than the 2026 model. That translates to a 0.3-second improvement in zero to 60 mph acceleration, to 3.7 seconds.


That in turn makes the 2027 SQ7 a second quicker to 60 mph than a Porsche Cayenne S and just 0.1 second behind a Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 S. That we’re talking about these numbers in the midsize luxury SUV segment is remarkable in and of itself, even if it’s hard to make use of that performance on public roads. Even if you’re not engaging launch control and fully sending it, the SQ7’s exhaust note is an attraction of its own. That familiar V8 rumble screams performance.


In addition to the V8, the SQ7 gets standard four-wheel steering, bigger brakes, and air suspension. Two versions of the latter are available: a comfort setup that’s similar to the optional system in the Audi Q7 on which the SQ7 is based, and a sport setup that sacrifices a bit of comfort for the best handling. The sport suspension is part of the S Sport Package, along with red brake calipers.


The sport suspension in our test car delivered the expected handling benefits, although on older pavement we lost patience with its firmer damping and switched back to the default Balanced drive mode (Comfort, Offroad, and Individual modes are also available). Four-wheel steering helped make the SQ7 feel nimbler than its size suggests, although it still feels like a big vehicle on narrow roads. It also doesn’t really feel awake at a normal pace, so you sometimes forget that you’re driving a twin-turbo V8 performance SUV. The SQ7 demands an autobahn.


## Form & function


8/10


The SQ7 is one of the few luxury performance SUVs to offer genuine three-row practicality. It comes standard as a seven-seater, with second-row captain’s chairs now optional for 2027. Audi didn’t just remove the middle seat from the second row; the individual seats were specifically designed for this application. They were both comfortable and supportive, although the seating position was a bit lower than expected.


The captain’s chairs also leave a convenient aisle for third-row access, and can power-tilt forward even with child seats installed. The third row is reasonably roomy for a midsize SUV, although it’s likely best reserved for kids. The redesigned body shell’s flatter roof and more upright D-pillar create more headroom than the outgoing model, Audi claims, but the step up to the third row (which sits directly over the rear axle, school bus back-seat style) might be a bit awkward for adults.


Both the second and third rows can fold with the press of a button. Cargo space should be similar to the SQ7’s less-sporty SQ7 sibling, meaning 15.1 cubic feet behind the third row, 37.7 cubic feet behind the second row with captain’s chairs (which don’t fold flat) or 43.9 cubic feet with the standard bench (which does), and 78.1 cubic feet behind the first row. The SQ7 can also tow up to 7,700 pounds when properly equipped, which is a very competitive number for a midsize luxury SUV.


Just as it doesn’t sacrifice any utility in the name of performance, the SQ7 doesn’t sacrifice any of the luxury the Q7 offers front-seat occupants. You get standard heated, ventilated, and massaging front seats. There’s also a decent-sized center console storage bin to ensure smaller items don’t go flying as you fling the SQ7 through the corners.


## Technology


8/10


The SQ7 comes standard with the same Audi Digital Stage tech setup as the Q7, meaning a trio of screens span the dashboard. An 11.9-inch digital instrument cluster and 14.5-inch touchscreen encircle the driver, while the front passenger gets their own 12.3-inch touchscreen with filters to avoid distracting the driver.


A head-up display is also available and front-seat occupants get high-speed magnetic wireless device chargers that stand a better chance of maintaining a connection during hard cornering. Second-row occupants get USB-C ports built into the back of the front seats, and third-row occupants have USB-C ports to plug into as well.


The 2027 SQ7 also upgrades to the current version of Audi’s MMI infotainment system, which is Android-based, but retains wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. We were also glad to see that Audi brought back Google Earth satellite maps, which can be shown across any of the screens. Other graphics were impressively as well, meeting expectations for a high-end SUV like this. The infotainment system was also as easy to use as it was to look at, although the front-passenger screen seems unnecessary. And in a 591-hp SUV, it could be a recipe for motion sickness depending on how enthusiastic the driver is.


However, those gorgeous Google maps are part of the Connect Nav digital services package, which comes as a three-year trial but requires a paid subscription after that. So is an intelligent voice recognition system with ChatGPT integration. When we couldn’t find the correct touchscreen menu, we simply asked it to turn on the seat massagers.


As with the 2027 Q7, the SQ7 can also be equipped with a 22-speaker, 1,360-watt, Bang & Olufsen 4D audio system as a standalone option. This system features headrests speakers that allow drivers to take phone calls without disturbing passengers, and in-seat actuators that let you feel the thump of the bass. The latter felt a little silly to us, but we know lots of people appreciate a bass-heavy system.


## Safety


7/10


Standard driver-assistance features on the 2027 Audi SQ7 include: forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking, blind spot monitoring, rear cross traffic alert, a 360-degree camera system, and lane departure warning. For 2027, the lane departure warning system has multiple settings for different road conditions, so you get fewer interventions when exercising the SQ7 on twisty roads.


A dashcam, surround-view camera system, driver-monitoring system, and adaptive cruise control with hands-free highway operation are also standard. The hands-free system can also make automated lane changes when the drive activates the turn signals. It worked well during our limited time with it.


Safety ratings from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) were not available at the time of writing.


## Cost-effectiveness


7/10


EPA fuel-economy ratings are what you should expect with a thirsty twin-turbo V8. At 17 mpg combined (15 mpg city, 20 mpg highway), the SQ7 isn’t doing the environment any favors. But the Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 S gets identical ratings, and the Porsche Cayenne S is rated only slightly higher. Porsche and Mercedes do offer plug-in hybrid versions of the Cayenne and AMG GLE, respectively, but you have to get the range-topping Cayenne Turbo E-Hybrid to beat the SQ7 in a drag race.


Pricing starts at $100,095 for the single available trim level with the mandatory $1,395 destination charge. Audi claims this is $1,100 less than a similarly-equipped 2026 model, but that difference won’t matter much once you start looking at options. The car we tested had 23-inch wheels, the high-end Bang & Olufsen audio system, and the Executive, Luxury, and Vision packages, bringing its as-tested price to nearly $120,000.


Even at that price, the SQ7 substantially undercuts the aforementioned Porsche Cayenne Turbo E-Hybrid, as well as the Cayenne GTS, which is slower from zero to 60 mph but more engaging to drive overall. The Cayenne S Electric offers similar performance to the Audi without guzzling gas, but it also starts a few grand more than a well-equipped SQ7. The Mercedes-AMG GLE 63 S starts almost $40,000 higher than a base SQ7, and the AMG GLE 53 Hybrid that more closely matches it in price isn’t as quick.


For similar money to a base SQ7, you could also have an all-electric Lucid Gravity Grand Touring. Unlike the other SUVs we’ve mentioned, it has a usable third row. It’s also a few tenths quicker from zero to 60 mph than the Audi, handles well, and has up to 450 miles of EPA range. But for those not ready for an EV, the redesigned SQ7 fills its niche well.
